reason_summary: No direct pre-modern causal estimate exists: demographic-significance.csv records n_cell_a_studies = 0 for PM, and the only PM-adjacent row is Basso, Bodenhorn and Cuberes, an 1850 cross-section of 196 counties rated serious for both confounding and selection, which is correlational rather than identified. No decomposition share, slope sufficiency or R-squared was computed for PM, and the mechanism as stated is a universal background condition that cannot explain cross-population variation. Discrepancy noted for the record: target-period-relevance.csv classifies Basso as PM|FDT while the demographic-significance table counts zero PM studies.

Two moderate-risk quasi-experiments converge (Danzer-Zyska Brazil, Rossi-Godard Namibia), and I verified that all three moderate-rated Cell A studies point the hypothesised way while the six serious-rated ones split three ways; but the FDT-proper historical studies are mutually inconsistent (Guinnane-Streb p=0.22, Fenge-Scheubel p about 0.09, Galofre-Vila positive) and the magnitudes are not comparable. I recomputed both pooled summaries: two studies hold 96.8% of the birth-probability weight and Billari-Galasso alone holds 88.3% of the completed-fertility weight, and adding back Galofre-Vila's excluded +0.098 children-ever-born estimate flips that pool from -0.0677 to +0.0549, so the pooled summaries cannot carry the FDT verdict. I also traced about 16 tier-2 papers with fertility outcomes and on-point titles, including Chile's 1981 privatization, Austria and several China pension reforms, that reached meta-analysis-ready status but never received an RA-review row, every one flagged NEEDS_MANUAL in the PDF manifest for no OA source, so replication across settings is unassessable; partial rests on Danzer-Zyska's 1.3-birth event-study magnitude, not on a computed threshold.

Rich-country SDT evidence reduces to one unpublished 2009 working paper, Billari-Galasso, whose completed-fertility estimate is 0.0529 with SE 0.0287; the only two replication candidates, Han and Shen, are both China, both serious risk of bias, both flagged policy-constrained by the project's own rule, and they point in opposite directions, an inconsistent pattern sitting on top of a single unreplicated quasi-experiment. I verified that Han's +4.0pp LTCI estimate is retained inside the birth-probability pool running against the channel's direction, on a treatment its own risk-of-bias rationale calls elder-care support rather than pension income. Not significant is a judgment from timing and direction, since mature systems leave no new margin and retrenchment predicts rising fertility against an observed fall, rather than from any computed share; escalating because demographic-significance.csv sets needs_human_review = yes and its required step of separating policy-constrained China from rich-country SDT is undone.

Revised up from my first pass after verifying the correction: exactly three studies carry OFF:different-channel in the adjudication and all three are in the chapter, they were high-scoring search hits at ranks 8, 10 and 19 with scores 9, 9 and 10 and two flagged gold anchors, and the near-miss, Bratti et al., is correctly excluded because its outcome is maternal labour supply, so the reinstatement was complete and carries no selection risk. Three quasi-experiments in three rich below-replacement countries, all moderate risk of bias, agree in direction after orientation, which meets the protocol's moderate pattern; the residual caveat the PI should see is that Eibich-Siedler's outcome is a birth in year t+1, a tempo measure, so the quantum margin is replicated by the Netherlands and Australia only. Demographic significance stays insufficient data because the sufficiency file states its own labels are not decomposition shares and the companion scaling file defers the real calculation to future work, with six of eight large labels dividing effects by TFR declines in incompatible units and one returning 273%; escalating because all eight Cell C effect rows are ra_verified = no while all sixteen Cell A and B rows are yes.
